card.title: WaterFlow
card.summary: A flow-matching generator and confidence model that predicts ordered water positions on protein structures, beating SuperWater at every precision level (parity F1 0.63 vs 0.41 at 1.0 Å). Adding crystal symmetry mates helps most, and many novel predictions sit on unexplained difference density, while diverse high-quality structures remain the main data limit.

nodes.title: QUE - Can a flow-matching model predict ordered water positions more accurately than the current state of the art?
nodes.desc: The previous best method, SuperWater, recovers only about 27% of waters at high precision. The paper asks whether a new generator and confidence model can do better, especially at sub-angstrom tolerance.
nodes.loc: Introduction, paragraphs 3 and 6; Results: Model Overview

nodes.title: QUE - How reproducible are deposited water molecules across otherwise identical crystal structures?
nodes.desc: If similar structures disagree on which waters are modeled, that variation limits any model trained and scored on deposited waters.
nodes.loc: Results: Crystallographic Water Placement Pareto Front, paragraphs 1-2

nodes.title: QUE - Is water prediction limited more by training data quantity or by data quality?
nodes.desc: The authors compare a larger, lower-resolution training set with a smaller, higher-quality one, and test filtering individual waters by quality.
nodes.loc: Results: Training data size affects prediction accuracy

nodes.title: QUE - Does adding crystal lattice neighbors (symmetry mates) to the input improve water prediction?
nodes.desc: Many surface waters are coordinated by atoms of neighboring molecules in the crystal, which a model that sees only the asymmetric unit cannot see.
nodes.loc: Results: Encoding Symmetry Mates Improves Prediction Accuracy, paragraph 1

nodes.title: QUE - Are predicted waters supported by the experimental X-ray data, not only by deposited models?
nodes.desc: Deposited models are incomplete, so a predicted water scored as a false positive may be a real water that was never built.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, paragraphs 1-2

nodes.title: QUE - How does WaterFlow behave across inference settings, on predicted structures and at ligand binding sites?
nodes.desc: Users choose a confidence or density threshold, and many applications will use predicted rather than crystal structures as input.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow Inference on Predicted Structures and Protein-Ligand Interactions

nodes.title: CLM - Water position prediction lags behind protein and protein-ligand structure prediction
nodes.desc: Protein structure prediction is near experimental accuracy for static structures, but water placement is still limited. Physics-based methods are slow and force-field dependent, and earlier deep learning methods remain weak at high precision.
nodes.loc: Introduction, paragraphs 2-3

nodes.title: CLM - Simpler design choices may suit the data-limited water prediction task
nodes.desc: WaterFlow uses flow matching instead of diffusion, a simpler atom-atom graph, ESM3 embeddings and GVP message passing. The authors speculate this passes information to water nodes more directly, but did not test each change.
nodes.loc: Discussion, paragraph 2; Results: Encoder, Generator, and Confidence Model

nodes.title: CLM - WaterFlow outperforms SuperWater at every precision level, most at sub-angstrom tolerance
nodes.desc: Both models were trained and scored on the same cluster-split data. The gap in parity F1 widens when the match radius is tightened from 1.0 to 0.5 Å.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow More Accurately Predicts Water Molecules, Figure 1B-C

nodes.title: CLM - Random train/test splits overstate water prediction accuracy because homologs share water sites
nodes.desc: SuperWater was originally trained and tested on random 8:1:1 splits. Retrained on sequence and structure cluster splits, its precision and recall were lower than first reported.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow More Accurately Predicts Water Molecules, last paragraph

nodes.title: CLM - Deposited ordered waters are a noisy target for training and evaluation
nodes.desc: Which waters are modeled varies with experimental conditions such as temperature and pressure, and with modeling choices, peak picking and phase bias. Real but unmodeled waters bound recall, and waters missing from the evaluated structure bound precision.
nodes.loc: Introduction, paragraphs 4-5

nodes.title: CLM - Consensus waters across isomorphous structures set an accuracy ceiling well above current predictions
nodes.desc: Up to about 30% of deposited waters are not reproduced across otherwise identical structures. The best achievable F1 against consensus sites is 0.87 to 0.94, so there is still room above WaterFlow.
nodes.loc: Results: Crystallographic Water Placement Pareto Front, Figure 2B

nodes.title: CLM - Consensus waters are better supported by the experimental data than non-consensus waters
nodes.desc: Consensus waters have lower B-factor z-scores and higher EDIA. Structures that agree more with the consensus have better resolution and lower R-free.
nodes.loc: Results: Crystallographic Water Placement Pareto Front, Figure 2C-D, Tables 2-3

nodes.title: CLM - Training only on well-supported waters should give a more accurate model (tested hypothesis)
nodes.desc: Because up to 30% of the training signal is unreliable, the authors hypothesized that restricting training to better-resolved and better-supported data would help.
nodes.loc: Results: Training data size affects prediction accuracy, paragraphs 1 and 3

nodes.title: CLM - Structural diversity of high-quality training data limits water prediction accuracy
nodes.desc: At equal training size, the higher-quality SMALL set gives better F1. LARGE overtakes it only by adding clusters that SMALL lacks, and then also saturates.
nodes.loc: Results: Training data size affects prediction accuracy, Figure 3A; Discussion, paragraph 4

nodes.title: CLM - Filtering individual training waters by EDIA and B-factor did not improve accuracy
nodes.desc: The model trained without the per-water filter was slightly better at parity. The authors suggest the extra waters may regularize, but say this needs more study.
nodes.loc: Results: Training data size affects prediction accuracy, Figure 3B; Discussion, paragraph 4

nodes.title: CLM - Models trained on static coordinates cannot represent partially occupied, fluctuating waters
nodes.desc: Many training waters are likely partially occupied and coupled to protein motion. Modeling protein, ligands and solvent as a joint ensemble could capture this.
nodes.loc: Discussion, paragraphs 9-10

nodes.title: CLM - Including symmetry mates in the input graph improves water prediction
nodes.desc: Symmetry mates restore the coordination environment of waters at crystal contacts. The gain is almost entirely for waters within hydrogen-bonding range of a lattice neighbor.
nodes.loc: Results: Encoding Symmetry Mates Improves Prediction Accuracy, Figure 4B-C; Discussion, paragraph 3

nodes.title: CLM - Explicit crystal symmetry may benefit structure prediction more broadly
nodes.desc: Only one prior model the authors found includes symmetry mates or crystal contacts. Proteins, ligands and ions also form contacts across symmetry-related interfaces.
nodes.loc: Discussion, paragraph 3

nodes.title: CLM - The confidence score tracks experimental density support of predicted waters
nodes.desc: Higher confidence thresholds give predicted waters with higher EDIAm and higher density. Above a threshold of about 0.7, predicted waters are as well supported as deposited ones.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, Figure 6A-B

nodes.title: CLM - Many novel predictions are real waters that deposited models omit
nodes.desc: Predicted waters with no deposited water within 1.0 Å often sit on positive mFo-DFc difference density, and always have more density support than nearby decoy positions.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, Figure 6B-E; Discussion, last paragraph

nodes.title: CLM - WaterFlow-predicted waters fit the structure factors nearly as well as deposited waters
nodes.desc: Unrefined predicted waters give R-free only slightly above the deposited model, and light refinement narrows the gap further. The authors suggest WaterFlow could be used to model waters during refinement.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, Figure 6F; Discussion, paragraph 10

nodes.title: CLM - Density thresholding removes the resolution dependence of water count at a small accuracy cost
nodes.desc: With a fixed confidence threshold, the number of predicted waters falls with resolution, as deposited counts do. Keeping a fixed number of top waters per residue avoids this, with slightly lower precision and recall.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow Inference on Predicted Structures, Figure 5A-B, Figure S5; README: Selecting the final waters

nodes.title: CLM - WaterFlow is less accurate on predicted structures than on crystal structures
nodes.desc: Predicted models carry a different distribution of coordinate error than refined crystal models, which can disturb hydrogen bonds. The confidence model likely needs recalibration for the input source.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow Inference on Predicted Structures, Table 4; Discussion, paragraph 7

nodes.title: CLM - WaterFlow is untested on cryo-EM structures and nucleic acids
nodes.desc: Training used only proteins from X-ray structures. Cryo-EM models have larger coordinate uncertainty, and waters around nucleic acids may fall outside the model's scope.
nodes.loc: Discussion, paragraph 8

nodes.title: CLM - WaterFlow can recover critical binding-site waters, including ligand-bridging waters
nodes.desc: In a matched apo/ATP-bound pair, WaterFlow placed bridging waters and the water shifted by the adenine ring close to their deposited positions. The authors note further testing is needed.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow Inference on Predicted Structures and Protein-Ligand Interactions, Figure 5E; Discussion, paragraph 5

nodes.title: EVD - Maximum precision/recall at 1.0 Å: 0.92/0.83 for WaterFlow vs 0.8/0.59 for SuperWater
nodes.desc: At 0.5 Å, WaterFlow fell only to 0.88/0.64 while SuperWater fell to 0.73/0.33. Best checkpoints: LARGE for WaterFlow, SMALL for SuperWater.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow More Accurately Predicts Water Molecules, paragraph 2; Figure 1B

nodes.title: EVD - Parity F1 at 1.0 Å: 0.63 for WaterFlow vs 0.41 for SuperWater; at 0.5 Å: 0.54 vs 0.26
nodes.desc: At parity and 1.0 Å, WaterFlow precision and recall were 0.64 and 0.63, against 0.42 and 0.41 for SuperWater.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow More Accurately Predicts Water Molecules, paragraph 3; Figure 1C

nodes.title: EVD - Consensus waters were 69.9% of HEWL, 86.5% of endothiapepsin and 78.5% of carbonic anhydrase waters
nodes.desc: Best clustering results. Ranges across hyperparameters were 63.2-70.4% (HEWL, n = 65), 83.6-86.5% (EAP, n = 907) and 77.8-79.1% (CA, n = 937).
nodes.loc: Results: Crystallographic Water Placement Pareto Front, paragraph 3; Supplementary Table 5

nodes.title: EVD - Pareto knee F1 against consensus sites: 0.87 (HEWL), 0.94 (EAP), 0.87 (CA)
nodes.desc: Precision/recall at the knee were 0.97/0.78, 0.92/0.96 and 0.88/0.86 at a 1.0 Å cutoff. Values fall slightly at 0.5 Å.
nodes.loc: Results: Crystallographic Water Placement Pareto Front, paragraph 4; Figure 2B; Figure S3

nodes.title: EVD - HEWL structures with fewest waters: precision 0.94, recall 0.36; with most waters: 0.47 and 0.85
nodes.desc: Ranges were 0.93/0.47 to 0.70/0.89 for EAP and 0.92/0.36 to 0.68/0.84 for CA. Modeling more waters trades precision for recall.
nodes.loc: Results: Crystallographic Water Placement Pareto Front, paragraph 4; Figure 2B; Supplementary Table 5

nodes.title: EVD - An EDIA cutoff of 0.4 would remove 20-26% of non-consensus waters but only 1-8% of consensus waters
nodes.desc: Consensus waters also have lower within-structure B-factor z-scores, in all three datasets (500-fold structure-level bootstrap).
nodes.loc: Results: Crystallographic Water Placement Pareto Front, paragraph 6; Figure 2D; Table 3

nodes.title: EVD - The half of structures with higher consensus F1 had better resolution and lower R-free in all three datasets
nodes.desc: Datasets were split at the median F1 (HEWL 0.71, EAP 0.85, CA 0.74) and compared with Mann-Whitney U tests.
nodes.loc: Results: Crystallographic Water Placement Pareto Front, paragraph 5; Figure 2C; Table 2

nodes.title: EVD - LARGE reached parity F1 63.4 at N = 60,116, against 61.0 for SMALL at its full 21,211
nodes.desc: Where training sizes overlap (601 to 21,211 structures), SMALL gives the better F1. LARGE has 15,573 clusters against 5,424 for SMALL.
nodes.loc: Results: Training data size affects prediction accuracy, paragraph 2; Figure 3A

nodes.title: EVD - Per-water filtering gave parity F1 63.4 against 63.8 without the filter
nodes.desc: The filter (EDIAm below 0.4 or B-factor z-score above 2.0) dropped 14.1% of LARGE waters. The unfiltered model was ahead by 0.50 F1 on average across the matched window.
nodes.loc: Results: Training data size affects prediction accuracy, paragraph 3; Figure 3B

nodes.title: EVD - Symmetry mates raised parity F1 at 1.0 Å from 0.57 to 0.63
nodes.desc: F1/precision/recall were 0.63/0.64/0.63 with mates and 0.57/0.57/0.57 without. The two models differ only in whether mates are in the graph.
nodes.loc: Results: Encoding Symmetry Mates Improves Prediction Accuracy, paragraph 2; Figure 4B

nodes.title: EVD - For waters within 3.4 Å of a symmetry mate, recall rose from 0.29 to 0.60
nodes.desc: These are about 10% of all waters. For waters farther than 3.4 Å from a mate, recall moved only from 0.62 to 0.67.
nodes.loc: Results: Encoding Symmetry Mates Improves Prediction Accuracy, paragraph 3; Figure 4C

nodes.title: EVD - One bridging water in 4RKW scored 0.004 without symmetry mates and 0.717 with them
nodes.desc: The mates add four potential hydrogen bonds (2.7-3.5 Å) to the single bond the water has within the asymmetric unit.
nodes.loc: Results: Encoding Symmetry Mates Improves Prediction Accuracy, paragraph 3; Figure S9

nodes.title: EVD - Median EDIAm of predicted waters rose from 0.40 at t = 0.10 to 0.85 at t = 0.90
nodes.desc: The deposited median is 0.78. Predicted waters match it at a confidence threshold of about 0.7.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, paragraph 2; Figure 6A

nodes.title: EVD - Novel waters above 3σ in mFo-DFc rose from 10.7% to 49.2% with increasing confidence threshold
nodes.desc: Median mFo-DFc of novel waters rose from 1.41σ to 2.97σ, and novel waters always had more density support than decoy positions.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, paragraph 3; Figure 6B

nodes.title: EVD - Three novel 4RKW waters sit on 9.1σ, 4.1σ and 4.1σ difference density
nodes.desc: The matched decoy positions sit at -2.3σ, -1.3σ and +1.7σ. Predictions at confidence threshold 0.5.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, paragraph 4; Figure 6C-E

nodes.title: EVD - Unrefined predicted waters gave 4RKW R-free 0.227 (t = 0.5) and 0.230 (ρ = 0.6) against 0.20 deposited
nodes.desc: After full refinement with water picking off, R-free was 0.203 and 0.210 against 0.191 for the deposited model. The gap narrowed from 0.027 to 0.012 for t = 0.5.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, paragraphs 5-6; Figure 6F

nodes.title: EVD - Density thresholding reached parity F1 0.596 against 0.634 for confidence thresholding
nodes.desc: With confidence t = 0.5, predicted water count correlated with resolution (R = -0.66), as deposited counts do (R = -0.61).
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow Inference on Predicted Structures, paragraphs 1-2; Figure 5A; Figure S5

nodes.title: EVD - On an ESMFold model of 4RKW (Cα RMSD 0.31 Å), precision and recall were lower than on the crystal structure
nodes.desc: MolProbity score was 1.69 against 1.24 (clashscore 14.1 against 4.65). Adding symmetry mates gave little to no improvement on the ESMFold model.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow Inference on Predicted Structures, paragraphs 4-6; Table 4; Figure 5D

nodes.title: EVD - In ATP-bound LuxO, 3 of 4 ATP-contacting waters were recovered, with both bridging waters within 0.1 Å
nodes.desc: The water displaced by the adenine ring was predicted 0.1 Å from its bound position, with no water predicted within 2.1 Å of its apo position.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow Inference on Predicted Structures and Protein-Ligand Interactions, paragraphs 7-8; Figure 5E

nodes.title: STU - WaterFlow against re-trained SuperWater on a 698-structure holdout
nodes.desc: Both models trained on LARGE and SMALL and scored on the same cluster-disjoint holdout (median resolution 1.90 Å, median R-free 0.212). Precision/recall swept over confidence thresholds.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluation Dataset; WaterFlow More Accurately Predicts Water Molecules

nodes.title: STU - Training-set size scaling on fractions of SMALL and LARGE
nodes.desc: The full pipeline was retrained on cluster-stratified fractions from 1% to 100% of each dataset. The three smallest fractions were repeated over three seeds.
nodes.loc: Results: Training data size affects prediction accuracy, paragraph 2; Figure 3A

nodes.title: STU - Per-water quality filter ablation on LARGE
nodes.desc: WaterFlow retrained on LARGE with and without removing waters with EDIAm below 0.4 or B-factor z-score above 2.0.
nodes.loc: Results: Training data size affects prediction accuracy, paragraph 3; Figure 3B

nodes.title: STU - Symmetry mate ablation
nodes.desc: Two LARGE-trained models that differ only in whether symmetry mates are in the input graph, compared at parity and by distance to the nearest mate.
nodes.loc: Results: Encoding Symmetry Mates Improves Prediction Accuracy; Figure 4; Figures S8-S9

nodes.title: STU - Consensus water clustering across isomorphous HEWL, endothiapepsin and carbonic anhydrase structures
nodes.desc: 65 HEWL, 907 endothiapepsin and 937 carbonic anhydrase structures with R-free better than 25%. HEWL reference was 7DER, and all HEWL structures were within 0.42 Å Cα RMSD of it.
nodes.loc: Results: Crystallographic Water Placement Pareto Front, paragraphs 2-3; Supplementary Tables 2-4

nodes.title: STU - Density support of predicted and novel waters across the holdout
nodes.desc: EDIAm of all predicted waters, and 2mFo-DFc and mFo-DFc levels at novel waters against decoy positions, across confidence thresholds.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, paragraphs 2-3

nodes.title: STU - DJ-1 (4RKW) case study of inference settings and novel waters
nodes.desc: WaterFlow on the 1.5 Å DJ-1 structure gave 157 waters at t = 0.5, 112 at ρ = 0.6 and 186 at ρ = 1.0.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow Inference on Predicted Structures, paragraph 3; Figure 5C; Figure 6C-E

nodes.title: STU - Refinement of 4RKW with predicted waters
nodes.desc: Predicted water sets and the deposited control were refined three ways: bulk-solvent rescaling only, water B-factors only, and full refinement.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, paragraphs 5-6; Figure 6F

nodes.title: STU - WaterFlow on an ESMFold model of DJ-1 against the 4RKW crystal structure
nodes.desc: Confidence and density inference with and without symmetry mates on both models. Mates for the ESMFold model used the 4RKW space group and unit cell.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow Inference on Predicted Structures, paragraphs 4-6; Table 4

nodes.title: STU - LuxO apo/ATP-bound binding-site waters (5EP1/5EP4)
nodes.desc: Both structures are 1.5 Å in space group P61. Waters within hydrogen-bonding range of binding-site residues and ATP were compared at t = 0.5 and ρ = 0.6.
nodes.loc: Results: WaterFlow Inference on Predicted Structures, paragraphs 7-8; Figure 5E

nodes.title: PRO - WaterFlow two-stage model: flow-matching generator and confidence model
nodes.desc: A GVP network on a protein-water graph with ESM3 residue embeddings. The generator learns a velocity field from prior samples to water positions; the confidence model, initialized from the generator, scores candidates against a target near 1 within 0.5 Å that decays to 0 by about 1.5 Å.
nodes.loc: Results: Encoder, Generator, and Confidence Model; Figure 1A; README: Training your own models

nodes.title: PRO - LARGE and SMALL datasets from PDB-REDO with cluster-based splits
nodes.desc: X-ray structures with 50-500 residues. LARGE: resolution 3.0 Å or better and R-free 0.20 or lower (67,272). SMALL: 2.0 Å or better and R-free 0.25 or lower (22,318). Clustered with MMseqs2 and Foldseek, and whole clusters assigned to splits.
nodes.loc: Results: Dataset; Table 1; Figures S1 and S7

nodes.title: PRO - Inference and scoring by precision@d, recall@d and parity F1
nodes.desc: Sample several-fold more candidates than expected, keep those above a confidence or density threshold, and cluster greedily within 1.52 Å. Score at d = 0.5 and 1.0 Å, with F1 at the point where predicted and deposited counts match.
nodes.loc: Results: Inference; Evaluation Metrics; README: Selecting the final waters

nodes.title: PRO - Symmetry mate expansion of the input graph
nodes.desc: Whole residues of symmetry-related copies, including ligands, ions and cofactors but not waters, with any atom within 8.0 Å of the asymmetric unit are added as protein nodes.
nodes.loc: Results: Encoding Symmetry Mates Improves Prediction Accuracy, paragraph 1; README: Step 2

nodes.title: PRO - HDBSCAN clustering of deposited waters to define consensus sites
nodes.desc: Align structures, cluster all deposited waters with HDBSCAN (hyperparameters ranked by DBCV and stability), and call clusters consensus when at least 30% of structures have a water within 1.0 Å.
nodes.loc: Results: Crystallographic Water Placement Pareto Front, paragraph 2; Figure 2A

nodes.title: PRO - Decoy null comparison of density at novel waters
nodes.desc: For each novel water, up to eight decoys are sampled on a 2.5 Å sphere around it, dropping any that overlap non-water heavy atoms. Density at novel waters and decoys is compared in 2mFo-DFc and mFo-DFc maps.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, paragraph 3

nodes.title: PRO - phenix refinement with predicted waters and water picking off
nodes.desc: Predicted waters start at B = 32.5 Å², the mean deposited water B-factor. Refinement runs with only water B-factors free, then with all coordinates, occupancies and B-factors, so no waters can be added or removed.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, paragraphs 5-6

nodes.title: REQ - Add more distinct, high-quality structures to the training data
nodes.desc: The authors name structural diversity of high-quality data as the most likely route to better water prediction.
nodes.loc: Results: Training data size affects prediction accuracy, last paragraph; Discussion, paragraph 4

nodes.title: REQ - Compare WaterFlow with physics-based solvation methods and displacement free energies
nodes.desc: Future work will test whether WaterFlow and methods such as 3D-RISM, GIST and inhomogeneous solvation theory agree on occupied sites, and whether confidence correlates with displacement free energy.
nodes.loc: Discussion, paragraph 6

nodes.title: REQ - Recalibrate the confidence model for predicted input structures
nodes.desc: Predicted and crystallographic coordinates are not equivalent, so the confidence model likely needs recalibration by input source.
nodes.loc: Discussion, paragraph 7

nodes.title: REQ - Evaluate WaterFlow on cryo-EM and nucleic acid structures
nodes.desc: Named by the authors as the focus of future work.
nodes.loc: Discussion, paragraph 8

nodes.title: REQ - Train water models with fluctuations, partial occupancy and joint protein-solvent ensembles
nodes.desc: The authors propose WaterFlow as a source of initial training data and suggest pairing it with experimental guidance such as sampleworks.
nodes.loc: Discussion, paragraphs 9-10

nodes.title: REQ - Test whether the binding-site and refinement results generalize beyond single examples
nodes.desc: The LuxO and 4RKW refinement results are each single demonstrations, and the authors state that further testing is needed.
nodes.loc: Results: Evaluating Water Prediction on Experimental Data, last paragraph; Discussion, paragraphs 5 and 10
